speaker: Bjarke Ingels
title: Bjarke Ingels - My evolutionary journey as an architect
question: In architecture, why does public and industry sentiment toward a once-celebrated studio often turn hostile after a couple of decades of growth?
guest: One thing that I've been struggling with lately is that your self-perception never changes. When we started, there was a lot of attention associated with our youth, and somehow in your mindset you never really change. Of course you learn a lot and discover things you didn't know, but your perception of yourself is pretty constant—in my case since I was 22. But the world starts seeing you differently. In the beginning they're rooting for the young challenger, but eventually they start booing at what they see as the establishment. It's not because you've become settled or established or tired of mind; it's just simply that you've been around for 25 years, we are 700 people, and we have a body of work. So there is a lot of harsh, uninformed opinions that you have to learn to take at a certain distance. Eventually, the harshness of the criticism isn't bad per se, even if it is often very uninformed, because at least it obligates you to be extra thoughtful and careful about your motivations and your actions.

points.core: A founder's internal self-perception stays largely constant across decades of firm growth.
points.note: Accept: founders still feeling like the same young challenger internally despite gaining experience over 20+ years. Do not credit: generic claims that successful founders become arrogant or out of touch.

points.core: Accumulated longevity automatically reframes a former challenger as the entrenched industry establishment.
points.note: Accept: simply surviving decades, scaling headcount, or amassing a large body of work flips public sympathy from cheering the underdog to attacking the incumbent without complacency or corruption. Do not credit: attributing backlash solely to declining design quality or controversies.

points.core: Harsh external criticism forces mature studios to scrutinize their own motivations rigorously.
points.note: Accept: even uninformed attacks usefully obligate leaders to be extra deliberate and careful about their actions while maintaining emotional distance. Do not credit: generic advice to listen to feedback or ignore critics.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The backlash usually comes from the gap between what made the studio admired and what growth forces it to become.

A young studio earns its reputation through a handful of fresh, risky, closely authored projects. Success brings bigger commissions from developers, corporations and governments, and with them larger teams, delegated design, and tighter budgets and schedules. The founder's hand thins out, and the signature ideas harden into a repeatable brand formula. What once looked radical starts to look like a product, applied regardless of place or context.

Meanwhile the studio's position shifts. It moves from outsider to establishment, so critics and younger architects define themselves against it. Its clients become more controversial (luxury towers, autocratic states, gentrifying megaprojects), which clashes with its early idealistic rhetoric. Early buildings also age, exposing leaks, cost overruns and maintenance problems, and large-firm labour practices such as long hours and low pay draw scrutiny.

Add simple overexposure and changing tastes, and the result is a familiar cycle seen with firms such as BIG, Zaha Hadid Architects, Foster + Partners, OMA and Heatherwick: novelty becomes ubiquity, and admiration becomes fatigue and resentment.

models.answer:
Celebrated architecture studios typically begin as scrappy, experimental challengers producing small, site-specific works that are easy to champion. Over two decades of growth, however, feeding a massive global payroll forces a structural shift toward high-fee commissions, including luxury speculative real estate, corporate monuments, and state-backed megaprojects for autocratic regimes. What started as inventive formal experimentation hardens into a repeatable signature brand dropped into cities regardless of local context, turning avant-garde freshness into diluted self-parody. 

Meanwhile, early breakthroughs age in public view, often revealing maintenance failures, cost overruns, or hostile streetscapes that erode civic goodwill. Within the profession, resentment builds as expansion exposes the gap between idealistic manifestos and corporate studio realities—grueling hours, low junior pay, greenwashing, and singular "starchitect" credit that obscures collective labor. Finally, cultural values evolve faster than architecture’s decade-long delivery cycles: projects conceived in an era of sculptural spectacle often open into a zeitgeist focused on housing affordability, adaptive reuse, and embodied carbon, recasting the once-rebellious firm as an entrenched symbol of establishment excess.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because growth changes what the studio is, while its reputation still rests on what it used to be. Early fame usually comes from a few daring, scrappy projects that seem to challenge the establishment. Twenty years later the firm has hundreds of staff, and that has several effects. The founder's signature hardens into a formula that gets repeated across many markets. Quality varies as design work is handed to large teams. The client list moves toward developers, tech giants and autocratic governments, and BIG's work on Saudi Arabia's NEOM and Zaha Hadid Architects' Gulf commissions drew this kind of criticism. In effect the studio has become the establishment it once seemed to oppose.

Time also exposes things. Early buildings show their leaks, cost overruns and maintenance problems. Utopian sales pitches start to look like branding. Stories about unpaid internships or long working hours come out. Meanwhile taste moves on. Critics and younger architects build their own standing by attacking the dominant aesthetic, and the press likes a fall from grace as much as a rise. The more the studio's image depended on one celebrity founder, the more personal and sharp the backlash tends to be.

When an architecture studio scales from an insurgent collective into a global powerhouse, the very forces that sustain its growth often erode the goodwill that built its reputation. Early on, small practices win admiration for experimental ideas, hands-on craft, and civic idealism. Over two decades, maintaining hundreds of employees requires chasing massive commissions—luxury developments, corporate campuses, and prestige megaprojects for controversial or authoritarian clients—which can make the firm appear compromised and detached from public need.

At the same time, rapid expansion forces founding principals into executive and marketing roles, turning once-radical formal inventions into repeatable, brand-friendly formulas. Inside the industry, resentment also builds around the grueling labor culture that frequently underpins high-profile studios. Finally, cultural values shift: aesthetic boldness that felt liberating twenty years ago can read as indulgent or tone-deaf amid climate urgency and housing scarcity. What began as an inspiring underdog eventually looks like the establishment, inviting both public fatigue and professional backlash.

Growth changes both what a studio builds and how people judge it. A distinctive approach can feel fresh in a handful of early projects and formulaic when it appears across dozens of buildings. Larger commissions also bring more decision-makers, tighter financial constraints and bigger consequences for the people who live nearby.

Those changes matter differently to peers and to the public. Architects who once admired a studio for challenging convention may come to see it as the firm that sets the convention. Residents may care less about its design language than about what a project replaces, who can afford to use it or whether it makes their street better. Because the architect’s name is visible, the studio can become the focus of anger over decisions shared with developers and city officials. The work may have changed, but so have the studio’s power and the expectations that come with it.
